etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From おおよそ (ōyoso).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From root shim-, cognate with classical verb 締む (shimu, “to fasten, tighten”) and modern verb 閉まる (shimaru, “to be closed”) + ふ (fu, auxiliary verb indicating repetition or ongoing action).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of だ (da, auxiliary expressing certainty) + けど (kedo, “although”).
Historically, also analyzed as a clipping of だけれども (da keredomo).
First cited to 1907.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Reduplication of もし (moshi), a shortened form of 申(もう)し (mōshi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 申(もう)す (mōsu, “to speak”, humble)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *osanki, variant of *wosanki. Possibly cognate with Goguryeo *烏斯含 (*osegam).It is highly likely a regional Wanderwort.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Japanese simplification of 圓, via a simplified character similar to 𠮚.
Specifically, starting in the beginning of the Meiji period, the 員 in the middle of the character was abbreviated to 丨 in handwriting. As time went on, the bottom stroke of 囗 gradually rose, until by the time of the adoption of the shinjitai characters, it had reached or even surpassed the box's centre.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/wen/ → /eɴ/
From Middle Chinese 圓 (MC hjwen), with the original sense of "circle, roundness".
The yen sense came much later in the Meiji period, from Chinese 圓 /圆 (yuán), itself from 銀圓 /银圆 (yínyuán, “round silver object(s), especially a piece of eight”). Compare Chinese 元 (yuán, “yuan”) and Korean 원 (won, “Korean won”). Doublet of 元 (gen, “yuan (Chinese currency)”), ユアン (yuan, “yuan (Chinese currency)”), and ウォン (won, “won (Korean currency)”).
The yen became the official currency of Japan in 1871, succeeding the 両(りょう) (ryō) and the 文(もん) (mon).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Various nanori readings.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 勘 (MC khomH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 匙 (zhiɛ, “spoon”). The goon, so likely the earliest borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 匙 (zhiɛ, “spoon”). The kan'on, so a later borrowing. Compare modern Cantonese 匙 (ci⁴), Min Nan 匙 (sî).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Likely an alteration of the kan'on reading shi: /si/ → /hi/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kapi₁/ → /kapi/ → /kaɸi/ → /kahi/ → /kai/
From Old Japanese 貝 (kai, “shellfish, clam; clam shell”), from the way that clam shells were used as scoops.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of 茶 (sa, “tea”, the tōon or Tang reading) + 匙 (ji, “spoon, scoop”). This on'yomi reading for a two-character term was then applied to the single-character 匙 spelling, and re-interpreted as kun'yomi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be an alteration of saji above: [sad͡ʑi] → [ɕad͡ʑi]

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Alternative spelling of 掬い (sukui, “scoop”), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 掬う (sukuu, “to scoop”).
Rare. Only found in compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Classical Japanese 咥(くは)ふ (kufafu). Possibly related to 食(く)う (kuu, “to eat; to grab with one's mouth”, historical form 食(く)ふ (kufu)), with auxilliary verb ふ (-fu), expressing repetition or ongoing state.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 家族 (MC kae dzuwk). However, not attested until 1808, so possibly a borrowing from modern written Chinese 家族 (jiāzú) with the expected Japanese reading applied.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Rearrangement of 和平 (wahei, “peace”), likely that 平 (hei) also means "flat", therefore switching the kanji meant "calm, equal + harmony → peace".
First attested in the Meiji era.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Chinese 平和 (pínghú).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kipʉ/ → /kiɸʉ/ → /kiu/ → /kʲɨː/
From Middle Chinese 急 (MC kip).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 成功 (d͡ʑiᴇŋ kuŋ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonpE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: See 指(ゆび) (yubi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 支配 (MC tsye phwojH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 暮(く)らす (kurasu, “to live, to lead a life”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 暮(く)らし (kurashi) above. The kurashi changes to gurashi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Possibly from Middle Chinese, or composed in Japan of Sinitic elements: 本 (hon, “main; real; the one under discussion”) + 人 (nin, “person”). Compare modern Mandarin 本人 (běnrén).
First cited to roughly 1215.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
水(みず) (mizu, “water”) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “wear, clothes”).
The ki changes to gi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1908.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 海水(かいすい) (kaisui, “seawater”) + 浴(よく) (yoku, “bathing”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Pseudo-loan from Chinese, a reformation of 物(もの)騒(さわ)がしい (monosawagashii, na-adjective). Alternatively, from 物忩(ぶっそう) (bussō).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese /*ʂamɑk̚/ > Japanese /*sabaku/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Old Japanese. Cognate with 面 (omote). Derived as a compound of 面 (omo, “face”) + 手 (te, “hand; direction, side”), basically meaning "face-wards; facing side".
The term omote in general is attested since the Nihon Shoki of 720. The 表 spelling for this word is attested from roughly 1000.
Cognate with Okinawan 表 (umuti).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 表 (MC pjiewX). Attested in a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 703.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)舞(ま)う (mimau).
Equivalent to 見(み) (mi) + 舞(ま)い (mai, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 舞(ま)う (mau)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 見(み) (mi) + 舞(ま)う (mau)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 規(き) (ki, “compass”) + 準(じゅん) (jun, “spirit level”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the classical lower bigrade verb (バ行下二段活用) のぶ (nobu). Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)べる (noberu) and 延(の)べる (noberu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 酔(よ)っ払(ぱら)う (yopparau).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 題 (MC dej|dejH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 額 (MC ngaek).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 食物 (zyik mjut, literally “eat + thing”). Possible alteration from strict goon reading jikimotsu, changing goon jiki for kan'on shoku.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 食物 (zyik mjut, literally “eat + thing”). Possible original reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Chinese 食物 (shíwù). Possible reborrowing, or change influenced by later contact with China after borrowing of earlier goon reading jikimotsu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 黄(き)色(いろ) (kiiro) + い (-i).
